cards.front: Why is routine preparticipation medical evaluation not mandated for all healthy individuals prior to beginning an exercise program?
cards.back:
Mandating routine clinical medical evaluations for everyone is limited by several factors:
  • Cost and System Capacity: Comprehensive medical evaluations are expensive, and the healthcare system lacks capacity to screen the entire population.
  • Unproven Risk Reduction: Routine medical evaluation in apparently healthy, asymptomatic populations has not been proven to reduce exercise-related medical risks.
  • Participation Barrier: Perceived medical evaluation requirements act as a significant barrier preventing sedentary people from becoming active.

cards.front: Why are simple height and weight measurements insufficient for evaluating body composition, and what model is used instead?
cards.back:
Height and weight alone (like BMI) fail to capture tissue distribution, relative adiposity, or fitness level. Instead, the two-compartment model is used to divide body mass into:
  • Fat Mass: Specifically tracking central/abdominal adiposity, which carries a strong association with cardiometabolic disease and disability.
  • Fat-Free Mass: Lean muscle and structural tissues that support metabolic health and functional capacity.

cards.front: What is the clinical significance of handgrip strength testing in older populations?
cards.back: Handgrip strength is an essential functional construct for activities of daily living and serves as a strong clinical predictor of functional independence and all-cause premature mortality in older adults.

cards.front: Why are sit-up and curl-up tests explicitly discouraged in health-related fitness testing, and what field test is recommended instead?
cards.back: Sit-up and curl-up tests are discouraged because they show only a moderate relationship to true abdominal muscular endurance and carry a high risk of causing lower back spinal injury. The recommended upper-body muscular endurance field assessment is the push-up test (maximal properly executed push-ups in 1 to 2 minutes).

cards.front: What muscles are evaluated by the sit-and-reach test, and what normative sex difference exists across flexibility assessments?
cards.back: The sit-and-reach test (trunk flexion test) measures the range of motion of the hamstrings and lower back musculature. On joint flexibility assessments, females almost routinely score significantly higher than age-matched males due to anatomical and connective tissue compliance differences.

cards.front: How is maximal oxygen consumption (VO2max) evaluated during submaximal graded exercise testing (GXT)?
cards.back: Submaximal GXT protocols measure steady-state heart rate (HR) at multiple increasing workloads. These measured HR data points are then linearly extrapolated to the subject's age-predicted maximal heart rate (HRmax) to estimate functional VO2max.

cards.front: What physiological variables are continuously monitored during a clinical diagnostic graded exercise test (GXT)?
cards.back:
A clinical diagnostic GXT involves progressive workload advancement every 1 to 3 minutes (typically up to 85% of estimated HRmax) with continuous monitoring of:
  • 12-Lead ECG: Evaluates cardiac rhythm, conduction abnormalities, and myocardial ischemia (e.g., ST-segment depression).
  • Systemic Blood Pressure: Verifies a normal linear rise in systolic BP alongside stable or slightly reduced diastolic BP.
  • Symptom Scales: Tracks rating of perceived exertion (RPE), chest pain/pressure (angina), dyspnea, and light-headedness.

cards.front: What diagnostic procedures are combined with a clinical GXT to improve cardiac disease detection, and how are test results classified?
cards.back:
To improve diagnostic specificity and sensitivity, clinical GXTs are combined with echocardiography, radionuclide myocardial perfusion imaging, or cardiovascular pharmacological stress agents. Test results are integrated and classified as:
  • Positive: Indicative of myocardial ischemia or coronary artery disease (CAD).
  • Negative: Normal physiological response without ischemia.
  • Equivocal: Uncertain results requiring follow-up invasive procedures like coronary angiograms.

cards.front: What is the sensitivity of a diagnostic test, and what is the average reported sensitivity of an exercise 12-lead ECG for detecting CAD?
cards.back: Sensitivity refers to a diagnostic test's ability to correctly identify individuals who actually have the disease in question. For exercise 12-lead ECG detection of coronary artery disease (CAD), sensitivity averages approximately 66%, meaning that 34% of individuals with CAD receive a false-negative result.

cards.front: Why is routine diagnostic exercise ECG testing rarely indicated for screening young, asymptomatic, healthy individuals?
cards.back:
Routine diagnostic exercise ECGs have low utility in low-risk, asymptomatic populations because:
  • Low Pre-Test Probability: In populations where disease prevalence is low, the positive predictive value of an abnormal test result is extremely low.
  • False Results: Low sensitivity (~66%) and low predictive value lead to high rates of false-negative and false-positive results, rendering routine GXT screening in healthy young populations ineffective.
